physical_harm: Deceased suffered severe injuries including severed limbs and fatal wounds; PW-2 sustained an injury on the left finger
number_of_offences: Nine accused named in FIR, three declared absconders, three juveniles, three prosecuted for murder
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the testimony of PW-1, the son of the deceased, and corroborated it with PW-2, the injured eyewitness, and PW-5, along with medical evidence and the presence of the dead body in the courtyard of accused-appellant no. 1.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that PW-1's testimony was corroborated by PW-5 and PW-2, and that PW-2's injury was medically confirmed by PW-4. The court rejected the suggestion that the witnesses were planted.

legal_representation.state: Vartika S. Walia (for Corporate Law Group)

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that all nine accused hacked the deceased with deadly weapons causing his death, dragged his body to the courtyard of one of the accused-appellants, and that the presence of the accused with weapons and their participation in dragging the body established their involvement in the crime.
defence_argument: The appellants contended that Section 34 IPC was not attracted as no overt act was attributed to them, there was no evidence of common intention, and the prosecution failed to establish any motive for the crime.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that common intention can be inferred from the conduct of the accused, including their presence with weapons, participation in the crime, and actions after the commission of the crime, as per the interpretation of Section 34 IPC.
precedent_relied_upon: Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1963 SC 174; Lal/an Rai and Others v. State of Bihar 2003 (1) SCC 268; Goudappa and Others v. State of Karnataka (2013) 3 sec 675; Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King Emperor AIR 1925 PC 1; Bairam Singh and Another v. State of Punjab AIR 2003 SC 2213; Atley v. State of U.P. AIR 1955 SC 807; State of Uttar Pradesh v. Kishanpal and Others 2008 (1.6) sec 73
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the appellants were found guilty of the murder, and the court affirmed the conviction and life imprisonment as a severe punishment for the brutal and premeditated crime.
